data.title: Trump administration to lend $100 million to telecoms firm Africell, countering Huawei in Africa
data.description:
By Alexandra Alper

The Trump administration will lend nearly $100 million to Africell, Africa's only American-owned telecoms firm, as the U.S. seeks to thwart the expansion of China's Huawei in Africa, according to a press release and a person familiar with the matter.

The loan from the Export-Import Bank will "enable Africell to invest in the latest mobile network technology from American and allied suppliers," according to the release, published on Friday and first reported by Reuters.

“We are pleased to be working with EXIM to introduce more trusted and secure communications infrastructure to our operating markets,” said Ziad Dalloul, CEO of Africell Holding Limited.

Huawei did not respond to a request for comment. The Chinese embassy in Washington said Chinese investment in Africa has spurred growth there and been welcomed by residents. It urged the U.S. to do more to support the development of other countries and not "pursue its Africa agenda with the aim of undermining China-Africa cooperation."

The loan is part of Washington's campaign to bolster the use of non-Huawei telecoms equipment overseas.

U.S. ALLEGES SPYING, HUAWEI DENIES

President Donald Trump's administration launched a "clean network" initiative in his first term to purge Chinese telecoms technology, apps and carriers from infrastructure in the U.S. and allied nations, and has continued similar efforts during his second term.

The U.S. has imposed heavy sanctions on Huawei over allegations the company could spy on users, which Huawei denies.

Huawei holds about a 52% market share for 5G infrastructure in Africa, according to Counterpoint Research.

The loan also follows through on a 2025 executive order by Trump mandating that U.S. agencies promote the use of U.S. technology abroad in AI as well as data center storage, cloud services and networking.

Founded in 2001, Africell bought technology from HP, Nokia, Dell, Oracle and others to power a new data center in Angola, according to its website. It serves 15 million customers across Angola, Gambia, the Democratic Republic of Congo and Sierra Leone.

Following a 2022 visit to Africell's Angola offices, former U.S. President Joe Biden's deputy secretary of state, Wendy Sherman, said that when countries choose Huawei, "they are potentially giving up their sovereignty ... turning over their data to another country."

Africell received a $100 million loan in 2018 from U.S. development financier the Overseas Private Investment Corporation, now the International Development Finance Corporation, to expand its communications infrastructure.

data.title: International Cotton Prices Rise as U.S. Crop Withers — Market Talk
data.description: International cotton prices rose in August, says Cotlook in a note. The firm says that its global price index rose to $1.013 a pound in August, which is the highest prices have been since May 2024. Driving the rising price is a host of factors, says Cotlook. "Bolls were opening in the key Xinjiang region, but uneven development was reported," says the firm. "Crop conditions deteriorated in the U.S. under hot, dry weather." The USDA will be releasing its next WASDE report at noon Eastern time, which will contain the latest production data for U.S. cotton crops. ICE cotton futures are down 1.1% to 87.26 cents a pound, but have gained 36% year-to-date. (kirk.maltais@wsj.com)

data.title: A Nation Remembers: 25 Years After 9/11, U.S. Mourns a Growing Number of Victims — WSJ
data.description:
By Jack Morphet and Joseph De Avila

America marks a quarter-century since the Sept. 11 attacks at remembrance ceremonies Friday, honoring the nearly 3,000 people killed when hijackers turned four jetliners into missiles in the deadliest terrorist attack on U.S. soil.

Families of victims gathered to read aloud the names of the men, women and children killed at the World Trade Center, the Pentagon and in a field near Shanksville, Pa., when an Islamic militants under the direction of al Qaeda leader Osama bin Laden staged the devastating coordinated strikes.

At the ceremony at Ground Zero in Lower Manhattan, Terry Strada, whose husband Tom Strada was killed in the attacks, called out successive U.S. administrations for failing to hold Saudi Arabia to account for its part in the terrorist attacks.

"My husband, Tom Strada, you are missed more with each year that passes," Strada said. "But how can it be 25 years and still we have no justice for the role that Saudi Arabia played in your murder?"

"It has been one betrayal after another," Strada said, adding "including leaders in front of us here today," drawing huge applause from the audience.

Former Presidents George W. Bush, Bill Clinton, Barack Obama and Joe Biden attended the Ground Zero ceremony in New York. Former New York Gov. George Pataki and former New York City Mayor Rudy Giuliani were also there, along with current Mayor Zohran Mamdani.

President Trump attended a wreath-laying ceremony at the Pentagon. The attacks displayed "the terrible power of hate," he said in a speech. But the aftermath demonstrated "the even greater power of the American spirit to endure and prevail and to win."

Strada, who is the national chair of 9/11 Families United, asked Vice President JD Vance, who attended the ceremony in New York, to carry her message back to Trump.

At the Ground Zero ceremony, six moments of silence marked the times each World Trade Center towers were struck and collapsed, and the times corresponding to the plane diving into the Pentagon in Arlington, Va., and the crash of United Airlines Flight 93 in rural Pennsylvania.

"This ceremony is essential" said Jim Giaccone, whose brother died in the attacks. "At the very least I get to come here, one day a year, and speak my brother's name-Joseph Michael Giaccone-out loud, and you hear it, and he is here, and he is present and he is never forgotten."

A seventh moment of silence-new this year-will honor those who died from illnesses stemming from the attacks, including first responders, residents and workers near the World Trade Center site who developed respiratory illnesses, cancer and other chronic conditions from exposure to toxins.

"The 9/11 attacks caused devastation that extended far beyond that single day," 9/11 Memorial & Museum Chairman Michael Bloomberg said. "Over the years, tens of thousands of first responders, construction workers, volunteers, and survivors have become ill and tragically, many have died."

More people have died from related illnesses in the past 25 years than those who were killed by the attacks on Sept. 11, Mamdani said earlier this week, while releasing a trove of documents that detailed air-quality issues and what the city knew about the toxic conditions after the towers fell.

Around 170,000 pages of documents showed that city officials knew the dangers posed by toxic chemicals in lower Manhattan despite publicly stating the air was safe, according to Benjamin Chevat, executive director of advocacy group 9/11 Health Watch, which sued for their release.

Researchers have found first responders and other workers at the World Trade Center site have a higher incidence of leukemia than the general population.

Bridget Gormley, 35, is the daughter of FDNY firefighter Billy Gormley, who contracted bladder cancer in 2016 and died in June 2017. She was 10 on Sept. 11, 2001. Her father worked at Ground Zero on what firefighters dubbed "the pile" - the rubble and steel heap of the collapsed Twin Towers - until it was fully extinguished nearly 100 days later.

"It's the full narrative now. 9/11 did not end on 9/11," she said, adding that entire neighborhoods in lower Manhattan where people went back to living and working were not safe. "These people have not finished dying."

Diane Massaroli, 59 years old, from Staten Island, attended the ceremony, wearing a badge with a picture of her late husband Michael Massaroli, who was a 38-year-old vice president of operations at Cantor Fitzgerald.

"This is where I have to be because no remains were ever found of him," Massaroli said. "You get through the rest of the year then once the end of August hits, you get that sick, nervous anxiety. It's a really sick feeling. I'm just a bundle of butterflies and nerves and by the end of the day you're just flat out exhausted."

Massaroli's son, who was six when his father died, and her daughter, who was two-months old at the time of the attack, accompanied her.

This article will be updated as news develops.
